newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Reluctant managers seen slowing East Europe mergers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Reluctant managers seen slowing East Europe mergers.

text.p: Several Central European companies are shopping for smaller firms as they seek to grow to compete with foreign competition, but no wave of big-ticket mergers is seen hitting the region soon.

Analysts said Polish paintmakers Polifarb-Cieszyn SA Polifarb-Cieszyn SA and Polifarb Wroclaw SA, whose shareholders vote this month on the first-ever merger of Warsaw-listed firms, may prove an exception.

Although similar deals were possible in the region, they said listed companies were more likely to continue recent attempts to acquire smaller, unlisted firms to strengthen their holdings against rising foreign competition.

"It's been small, or sometimes it's not been full mergers, it's been stake-taking, but the signs are we will be having increasing merger activity," said Andrea Kirkby, Senior Regional Equity Analyst at Daiwa in London.
Kirkby said two or three mergers of Warsaw-listed firms could happen later this year but that acquisitions by Central European firms in less developed countries further east were even more likely.

"When you see so many strong Polish and Hungarian firms...doing a lot of business in Ukraine and the CIS, then you think it's not going to be very long until some of them at least set up production there," Kirkby said.
"And so far they've been saying, 'Well, maybe a greenfield site and maybe an acquisition,' but if privatisation in countries further east proceeds faster, then it may be by acquisitions."
SMALL FIRMS NEED TO COMBINE TO DEFEND MARKET SHARE
Analysts said firms in the region, small compared to their Western counterparts, needed to combine to defend market share versus the foreign presence.

The Polifarbs were seen as responding to Dutch Akzo Nobel's recent buy of another Polish paintmaker. Analysts said that despite their merger, the Polifarbs might still need a foreign strategic investor in two or three years to compete against the likes of Akzo, which might expand further.
MANAGERS SEEN IMPEDING MERGERS
Despite the need for relatively small Central European firms to combine, some analysts said mergers might be blocked by managers jealous of their new powers in a free market.

"They (mergers) will be rather scarce in the near future because newly independent managers are going to be very loath to surrender their independence unless they are forced to by extreme circumstances," said Maciej Olex-Szczytowski, Dresdner Kleinwort Benson head for Central Europe.
Olex-Szczytowski said such extreme circumstances would more likely lead to firms securing a foreign strategic investor than suffering the loss of face of selling out to a local rival.

Some said the combining of the Polifarbs, which hope to merge mid-year, might prove an exception because a relatively large mutual shareholder, B.I.G Industries Bhd, was influential in bringing them together.

They said the lack of a strong mutual shareholder in two potentially merging firms could prevent fusions from happening, as dispersed small shareholders were not likely to exert sufficent pressure on management.

Wojtek Janczyk, managing director of the small investment bank Business Management and Finance SA, said mergers might prove common only in situations such as Poland's mass privatisation National Investment Fund (NFI) programme.
The scheme has given the NFIs -- 15 foreign and domestic-run management firms -- control of some 500 medium-size enterprises.

"Mergers can happen in NFIs because...it's easy to force the managements to work together, to tell them, 'We will merge the company, you will be the dominant player, you will be the company head office'," Janczyk said.
Daiwa's Kirkby said Central European managements were little different from those elsewhere and would be willing to merge if they could see an increase in shareholder value.
BREWERS AND BANKS MERGING
Kirkby noted the acquisition plans of Polish food and construction firms and the jockeying between Britain's Bass Plc and Plzensky Prazdroj a.s. in the Czech Republic.
Bass, which has a majority stake in Prazske Pivovary s.a., seeks to increase its 33 percent share in Radegast and then possibly merge the two, gaining a 30 percent market share.
Plzensky Prazdroj, the largest Czech brewer, has shown interest in buying fifth-largest Jihoceske Pivovary to capture a similar percentage of the market.
"The consolidation process is inevitable...mid-size breweries will really face difficulties," said Jiri Kraus, a beer industry analyst at ING Barings in Prague.
In Hungary, Austrian beverage group Brau Union AG has said it will merge its two Hungarian breweries, Elso Magyar Szovetkezeti Sorgyar Rt and Soproni Sorgyar.
Analysts also see consolidation among the region's banks, which are trying to combine their capital ahead of the sector's full opening to foreign competition later in the decade.
The Warsaw bourse's large financial sector has already seen BPH, PBR, Kredyt Bank and insurer Warta forming a capital group with privatising Powszechny Bank Kredytowy SA (PBK).

BIG, has taken a majority stake in Bank Gdanski while Bank Pekao SA and three other state-owned banks were lumped together by the Finance Ministry to form a capital group earmarked for a partial sell-off in 1998.

In the Czech Republic, smaller banks are seen consolidating to compete against the country's four largest entities while some analysts in Slovenia expect the number of banks there to shrink to five or six by the end of the decade from about 30 today.
FEAR OF HOSTILE TAKEOVER
Tomasz Berent, an analyst at IB Austria Securities in Warsaw, saw potential mergers in the fragmented Polish construction industry, where no firm holds more than a one-percent market share.
He said the mergers could be spurred by the fear of hostile takeover, with the relatively large free-float of some of the larger builders making them ripe for taking.
Kirkby said such a fear might have played a role in the Polifarb merger.
"Whether or not it was intended to be, it is a pretty good defensive strategy -- it's going to be very difficult to take over that size of player," she said.
